author: Italo Calvino

it.text: I classici sono quei libri di cui si sente dire di solito: «Sto rileggendo...» e mai «Sto leggendo...».
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Perché leggere i classici» (Mondadori, Milan, 1995 edition)

en.text: The classics are the books of which we usually hear people say: “I am rereading…” and never “I am reading….”
en.source_note: “Why Read the Classics?”, translated by Patrick Creagh, The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986 (English translation © 1986 Harcourt Brace Jovanovich)

notes: Definition 1 of the essay.

author: Italo Calvino

it.text: Un classico è un libro che non ha mai finito di dire quel che ha da dire.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Perché leggere i classici» (Mondadori, Milan, 1995 edition)

en.text: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
en.source_note: “Why Read the Classics?”, translated by Patrick Creagh, The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986 (English translation © 1986 Harcourt Brace Jovanovich)

notes: Definition 6 of the essay.

author: Carlo Collodi

it.text: C'era una volta... – Un re! – diranno subito i miei piccoli lettori. – No, ragazzi, avete sbagliato. C'era una volta un pezzo di legno.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Le avventure di Pinocchio», Incipit

en.text: Centuries ago there lived— “A king!” my little readers will say immediately. No, children, you are mistaken. Once upon a time there was a piece of wood.
en.source_note: The Adventures of Pinocchio, translated by Carol Della Chiesa; Project Gutenberg EBook #500 (official PG mirror), chapter 1

notes: Opening lines of the novel. The translation renders «C'era una volta...» as «Centuries ago there lived—».

author: Cesare Pavese

it.text: Leggendo non cerchiamo idee nuove, ma pensieri già da noi pensati, che acquistano sulla pagina un suggello di conferma.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Il mestiere di vivere», diary entry of 3 December 1938

en.text: When we read, we are not looking for new ideas, but to see our own thoughts given the seal of confirmation on the printed page.
en.source_note: This Business of Living (diary 1935–1950), translated by A. E. Murch with Jeanne Molli; entry of 3 December 1938

notes: First sentence of the diary entry; the entry continues. Diary published posthumously (1952).

author: Dante Alighieri

it.text: In quella parte del libro de la mia memoria dinanzi a la quale poco si potrebbe leggere, si trova una rubrica la quale dice: Incipit vita nova.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Vita nuova», Incipit (chapter I)

en.text: In that part of the book of my memory before the which is little that can be read, there is a rubric, saying, Incipit Vita Nova.
en.source_note: The New Life, translated by Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1861); en.wikiquote links the Project Gutenberg text (EBook #41085)

notes: Opening of the Vita nova; the year is approximate (written c. 1293–1295). «Incipit vita nova» is Latin in both versions.

author: Dante Alighieri

it.text:
O de li altri poeti onore e lume,
vagliami ’l lungo studio e ’l grande amore
che m’ha fatto cercar lo tuo volume.
it.source_note: La Divina Commedia, Project Gutenberg EBook #1000 (official PG mirror), Inferno, canto I

en.text:
O, of the other poets honour and light,
Avail me the long study and great love
That have impelled me to explore thy volume!
en.source_note: The Divine Comedy, translated by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1867), Project Gutenberg EBook #1001 (official PG mirror), Inferno, canto I

notes: Dante addressing Virgil. Verse line breaks kept as \n; the opening quotation mark of the speech («, “) was left out because the excerpt stops mid-speech. Year is approximate (Inferno c. 1314).

author: Edmondo De Amicis

it.text: Per lui, ad ogni nuovo libro che compera, è una festa a lisciarlo, a metterlo al posto e a riprenderlo per guardarlo per tutti i versi e a covarselo come un tesoro.
it.source_note: Italian Wikisource, Cuore (Treves, 1889 edition), Gennaio, «La libreria di Stardi»; Wikisource page marker [p. 83] removed

en.text: It is a festival for him to polish off every new book that he buys, to put it in its place, and to pick it up again to take another look at it from all sides, and to brood over it as a treasure.
en.source_note: Cuore (Heart): An Italian Schoolboy's Journal, translated by Isabel F. Hapgood (1887), Project Gutenberg EBook #28961 (official PG mirror), «Stardi's Library»

notes: The schoolboy Stardi and his small home library.

author: Edmondo De Amicis

it.text: S’è fatto il suo catalogo. È come un bibliotecario.
it.source_note: Italian Wikisource, Cuore (Treves, 1889 edition), Gennaio, «La libreria di Stardi»

en.text: He has made himself a catalogue. He is like a librarian.
en.source_note: Cuore (Heart): An Italian Schoolboy's Journal, translated by Isabel F. Hapgood (1887), Project Gutenberg EBook #28961 (official PG mirror), «Stardi's Library»

notes: Same chapter as the previous De Amicis entry; «he» is the schoolboy Stardi, who catalogues his books. Very short: works well on a welcome screen if the work title is shown.

author: Primo Levi

it.text: Infatti, come c'è un'arte di raccontare, solidamente codificata attraverso mille prove ed errori, così c'è pure un'arte dell'ascoltare, altrettanto antica e nobile, a cui tuttavia, che io sappia, non è stata mai data norma.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «La chiave a stella»

en.text: In fact, just as there is an art of story-telling, strictly codified through a thousand trials and errors, so there is also an art of listening, equally ancient and noble, but as far as I know, it has never been given any norm.
en.source_note: The Monkey's Wrench, translated by William Weaver, Summit Books, New York, 1986 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; confirmed in a second scan, monkeyswrench0000levi_v3q3)

notes: Line-break hyphen in the scan («an- cient») joined as «ancient»; «story-telling» is hyphenated in both scans.

author: Umberto Eco

it.text: Sino ad allora avevo pensato che ogni libro parlasse delle cose, umane o divine, che stanno fuori dai libri. Ora mi avvedevo che non di rado i libri parlano di libri, ovvero è come si parlassero fra loro.
it.source_note: Il nome della rosa (Bompiani), Internet Archive scans bwb_KV-166-631 and umbertoecoilnome0000vari, text read via full-text search; Quarto giorno

en.text: Until then I had thought each book spoke of the things, human or divine, that lie outside books. Now I realized that not infrequently books speak of books: it is as if they spoke among themselves.
en.source_note: The Name of the Rose, translated by William Weaver, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, San Diego, 1983 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search)

notes: Adso speaking. OCR line-break hyphen «stan- no» joined as «stanno». The wording «è come si parlassero» (without «se») is confirmed by both scans and by several scholarly books quoting the passage.

author: Goliarda Sapienza

it.text: Non c'è niente da fare, come diceva mia madre, ogni dieci anni bisogna rileggere i libri che ci hanno formato se si vuol venire a capo di qualcosa.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «L'arte della gioia», chapter 63

en.text: It can’t be helped, as my mother used to say: every ten years we must re-read the books that shaped us if we want to understand anything.
en.source_note: The Art of Joy, translated by Anne Milano Appel, Farrar, Straus and Giroux, New York, 2013 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; same text in a second scan, artofjoy0000sapi)

notes: Spoken by a character in dialogue; the closing quotation mark of the speech was left out. Novel written 1967–1976, published in full posthumously (1998).

author: Italo Svevo

it.text: È così che a forza di correr dietro a quelle immagini, io le raggiunsi. Ora so di averle inventate. Ma inventare è una creazione, non già una menzogna.
it.source_note: Original Italian as given by en.wikiquote, from La coscienza di Zeno, ed. Cristina Benussi (Feltrinelli, 2004), p. 337

en.text: Thus, after pursuing those images, I overtook them. Now I know that I invented them. But inventing is a creation, not a lie.
en.source_note: Zeno's Conscience, translated by William Weaver (Penguin, 2002), p. 404, as quoted by en.wikiquote

notes: Zeno on the memories he has written down: inventing as creation. Italian taken from en.wikiquote's bilingual entry (it.wikiquote not checked for this line).

author: Dino Buzzati

it.text: Così una pagina lentamente si volta, si distende dalla parte opposta, aggiungendosi alle altre già finite, per ora è solamente uno strato sottile, quelle che rimangono da leggere sono in confronto un mucchio inesauribile.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Il deserto dei Tartari», chapter 17

en.text: So a page is slowly turned, falls over to join the others, the ones already finished. It is still only a thin layer. Those still to be read are inexhaustible in comparison.
en.source_note: The Tartar Steppe, translated by Stuart C. Hood, Carcanet, Manchester, 1987 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; same text in the David R. Godine 1995 edition scan, tartarsteppe00buzz_0)

notes: In the novel the pages stand for the days of a life; the next sentence («Ma è pur sempre un'altra pagina consumata... una porzione di vita» / «But it is always another page finished, a portion of your life») was left out to stay under 300 characters and keep the tone light. Line-break hyphen («compar- ison») joined.

author: Umberto Saba

it.text: Amai trite parole che non uno / osava. M'incantò la rima fiore / amore, / la più antica difficile del mondo.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, poem «Amai» (Il Canzoniere, p. 514); Wikiquote's line separators « | » rendered as « / »

en.text: I loved trite words that no one / dared. The rhyme fiore / amore enchanted me, / the most ancient and difficult in the world.
en.source_note: Translation by Joseph Cary in Three Modern Italian Poets: Saba, Ungaretti, Montale (New York University Press, 1969; same text in the 1993 reissue), Internet Archive scans, text read via full-text search; slashes mark line breaks in the source

notes: Opening lines of the poem. Cary keeps the rhyme words «fiore / amore» in Italian. Another published rendering (The Green Flame, 1987 anthology) is freer: «I loved familiar words which no one dared use. I loved the rhyme love dove, the oldest and most difficult in the world.»

author: Elena Ferrante

it.text: Io credo che i libri non abbiano alcun bisogno degli autori, una volta che siano stati scritti. Se hanno qualcosa da raccontare, troveranno presto o tardi lettori, se no, no.
it.source_note: Quoted in l'Unità, 14 November 2003 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search); OCR «lo credo» read as «Io credo»

en.text: I believe that books, once they are written, have no need of their authors. If they have something to say, they will sooner or later find readers; if not, they won't.
en.source_note: As quoted in Rebecca Lee, How Words Get Good (Profile Books, London, 2022); the first sentence also in The Guardian, 19 March 2022 (Internet Archive scans). The quoting sources do not name the translator; the English Frantumaglia (Europa Editions, 2016) is by Ann Goldstein (not verified here).

notes: Italian is a newspaper quotation of the letter, not the book itself, so punctuation may differ slightly from La frantumaglia (e/o). From the 1991 letter explaining why she would not appear in public.

author: Elsa Morante

it.text: Le serate invernali, e i giorni di pioggia, io li occupavo con la lettura. Dopo il mare, e i vagabondaggi per l’isola, la lettura mi piaceva più di tutto. Per lo più leggevo in camera mia, sdraiato sul letto, o sul canapè, con Immacolatella ai miei piedi.
it.source_note: L'isola di Arturo, Einaudi, Turin (1995 edition; same text in the 1957 edition scan lisoladiarturoro0000mora_d9j9), Internet Archive, text read via full-text search

en.text: On winter evenings, or when it rained, I spent the time reading. After the sea and wandering about the island, reading was what I liked best. Generally I read in my rooms, lying on the bed or on a sofa, with Immacolatella at my feet.
en.source_note: Arturo's Island, translated by Isabel Quigly, Alfred A. Knopf, New York, 1959 (same text in the 2002 Steerforth Italia reissue), Internet Archive scans, text read via full-text search

notes: Arturo, the narrator, as a boy on Procida; Immacolatella is his dog. Not on Wikiquote: both texts come from book scans, each confirmed in two editions.

author: Alessandro Manzoni

it.text: Don Ferrante passava di grand'ore nel suo studio, dove aveva una raccolta di libri considerabile, poco meno di trecento volumi: tutta roba scelta, tutte opere delle più riputate, in varie materie; in ognuna delle quali era più o meno versato.
it.source_note: I promessi sposi (illustrated 1840 edition text), Project Gutenberg EBook #45334 (official PG mirror), chapter XXVII

en.text: Don Ferrante passed much time in his study, where he had a considerable collection of choice books; he had selected the most famous works on many different subjects, in each of which he was more or less versed.
en.source_note: The Betrothed, anonymous translation, Richard Bentley, London, 1834 (Standard Novels no. XLIII), Project Gutenberg EBook #35155 (official PG mirror)

notes: The 1834 translation was made from the 1827 text and leaves out «poco meno di trecento volumi» (nearly three hundred volumes). In the novel Don Ferrante is a gently mocked pedant; the sentence on its own reads as a portrait of a home library.

author: Giacomo Leopardi
work: Operette morali, «Detti memorabili di Filippo Ottonieri»

it.text: E dimandandolo alcuni perchè non prendesse a filosofare anche in iscritto, come soleva fare a voce, e non deponesse i suoi pensieri nelle carte, rispose: il leggere è un conversare, che si fa con chi scrisse.
it.source_note: Opere, ed. Antonio Ranieri, Le Monnier, Florence, 1851, vol. II (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search); same words in the 1998 Lavoro edition of the Detti memorabili and in the 1827 and 1834 editions of the Operette morali

en.text: Being asked one day why he did not give written as well as verbal expression to his philosophical views, he replied: Reading is a conversation held with the writer.
en.source_note: «Remarkable Sayings of Philip Ottonieri», in Essays and Dialogues of Giacomo Leopardi, translated by Charles Edwardes, Trübner, London, 1882; Project Gutenberg EBook #52356 (official PG mirror)

notes: Ottonieri is Leopardi's fictional philosopher. The English quotation continues after «writer.», so its opening quotation mark was left out. Shorter form if preferred: «il leggere è un conversare, che si fa con chi scrisse» / «Reading is a conversation held with the writer.»

author: Vittorio Alfieri
work: Del principe e delle lettere (book I, chapter 8)

it.text: Leggere, come io l'intendo, vuol dire profondamente pensare; pensare, vuol dire starsi; e starsi, vuol dire sopportare.
it.source_note: Opere di Vittorio Alfieri ristampate nel primo centenario della sua morte, Paravia, 1903 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search); first clause also on Italian Wikiquote (https://it.wikiquote.org/wiki/Vittorio_Alfieri, «Del principe e delle lettere», I, 8)

en.text: To read, as I understand it, means to think deeply; to think deeply means to stand firm, and to stand firm means to endure.
en.source_note: The Prince and Letters, translated by Beatrice Corrigan and Julius A. Molinaro, University of Toronto Press, 1972 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search)

notes: Medium because the full Italian sentence was read from OCR: «Y intendo» corrected to «l'intendo» and stray spaces before semicolons removed; editions differ slightly in commas (the 1859 Barbèra edition has «pensare vuol dire starsi; e starsi vuol dire sopportare»). The first clause alone is confirmed by Italian Wikiquote. The context is political (readers as the prince's enemy), but the sentence itself is not.

author: Alessandro Baricco

it.text: Forse leggere migliaia di libri non è poi così inutile, pensò.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Mr Gwyn»

en.text: Maybe reading thousands of books isn’t so useless, she thought.
en.source_note: Mr Gwyn, in Mr Gwyn & Three Times at Dawn, translated by Ann Goldstein, McSweeney's, San Francisco, 2014 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search)

notes: Rebecca's thought about Mr Gwyn (the sentence before: «Era incredibile come quell'uomo avesse capito tutto senza praticamente fare una sola domanda.»). Light, slightly ironic tone.

author: Erri De Luca

it.text: Leggo solo libri usati.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Tre cavalli», Incipit (opening sentence of the novel)

en.text: I only read used books.
en.source_note: Three Horses, translated by Michael F. Moore, Other Press, New York, 2005 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search); the first words are set in small capitals («I ONLY READ USED books.»)

notes: Opening sentence of the novel; very short. The narrator goes on: used books stay open against the bread basket while he eats. The Italian continuation could not be checked in a reliable source, so only the first sentence is given.

author: Antonio Tabucchi

it.text: Disse: la filosofia sembra che si occupi solo della verità, ma forse dice solo fantasie, e la letteratura sembra che si occupi solo di fantasie, ma forse dice la verità.
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Sostiene Pereira», chapter IV (Feltrinelli, 2010, p. 30), which starts the quote at «la filosofia»; the full sentence with «Disse:» checked in the Feltrinelli 1996 scan on the Internet Archive (sostienepereirau0000tabu)

en.text: He said: Philosophy appears to concern itself only with the truth, but perhaps expresses only fantasies, while literature appears to concern itself only with fantasies, but perhaps it expresses the truth.
en.source_note: Pereira Declares: A Testimony, translated by Patrick Creagh, New Directions, New York, 1995 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; same text in declarespereirat0000tabu and pereiramaintains0000tabu)

notes: Pereira quoting a saying of his uncle, «a failed man of letters». A printed page number inside the English sentence in the scan was dropped. If «Disse: / He said:» reads oddly on screen, Wikiquote's shorter form starts at «la filosofia...», and the English at «Philosophy appears...».

author: Natalia Ginzburg

it.text: Questo è, in parte, quel libro: ma solo in parte, perché la memoria è labile, e perché i libri tratti dalla realtà non sono spesso che esili barlumi e schegge di quanto abbiamo visto e udito.
it.source_note: Lessico famigliare, Einaudi, 1999 printing, author's note «Avvertenza» (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; same wording in the 1963 Einaudi scan, lessicofamigliar0000unse)

en.text: This is to some extent that book, but only to some extent, because memory is treacherous and books founded on reality are so often only faint reflections and sketches of all that we have seen and heard.
en.source_note: Family Sayings, revised from the original translation by D. M. Low, Carcanet Press, Manchester, 1984, author's preface (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search)

notes: «That book» is the book about the people of her youth that she had always wanted to write. Second Ginzburg entry; use only one if needed.

author: Umberto Eco
work: Come si fa una tesi di laurea

it.text: Non credete a coloro che dicono che i libri vanno rispettati. I libri si rispettano usandoli, non lasciandoli stare.
it.source_note: Come si fa una tesi di laurea, Bompiani, Milan, 2001 printing (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search); the second sentence is also on Italian Wikiquote (https://it.wikiquote.org/wiki/Umberto_Eco, p. 139)

en.text: Do not trust those who say that you must respect books. You respect books by using them, not leaving them alone.
en.source_note: How to Write a Thesis, translated by Caterina Mongiat Farina and Geoff Farina, MIT Press, Cambridge MA, 2015 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; a running page header between «using them,» and «not leaving them alone» was dropped)

notes: Eco's advice to annotate the books you own (the paragraph opens: «If the book is yours and it does not have antiquarian value, do not hesitate to annotate it»).

author: Patrizia Cavalli
work: Le mie poesie non cambieranno il mondo (opening poem)

it.text: Qualcuno mi ha detto che certo le mie poesie non cambieranno il mondo. Io rispondo che certo sì le mie poesie non cambieranno il mondo.
it.source_note: Bilingual anthology New Italian Poets, ed. Dana Gioia and Michael Palma, Story Line Press, 1991 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search); same Italian in The FSG Book of Twentieth-Century Italian Poetry (2012)

en.text: Someone told me that of course my poetry won't change the world. I answer that of course not my poetry won't change the world.
en.source_note: Translated by Judith Baumel, in New Italian Poets (Story Line Press, Brownsville OR, 1991), Internet Archive scan read via full-text search

notes: Whole poem (six short lines in the original); both texts are given without line breaks because full-text search drops them. A light, self-ironic piece about poetry rather than books. Barry Callaghan's version in the FSG anthology reads: «I was told there's no way my poems will change the world. Yes I say my poems will in no way change the world.»

author: Galileo Galilei
work: Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo (Giornata prima)

it.text: Ma sopra tutte le invenzioni stupende, qual eminenza fu quella di colui che s'immaginò di trovar modo di comunicare i suoi più reconditi pensieri a qualsivoglia altra persona, benché distante per lunghissimo intervallo di luogo e di tempo?
it.source_note: Italian Wikiquote, section «Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi», linked to Wikisource, Giornata prima

en.text: But surpassing all stupendous inventions, what sublimity of mind was his who dreamed of finding means to communicate his deepest thoughts to any other person, though distant by mighty intervals of place and time!
en.source_note: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, translated by Stillman Drake, University of California Press, 2nd edition 1967 (Internet Archive scan, text read via full-text search; same text in the 1953 and 1962 printings)

notes: Sagredo praising the inventor of the alphabet. Only the first sentence is used; in Drake's version the passage goes on to talking with those in India and those not yet born, «and with what facility, by the different arrangements of twenty characters upon a page!»

author: Carlo Collodi

it.text: Dopo poco tornò: e quando tornò, aveva in mano l'Abbecedario per il figliuolo, ma la casacca non l'aveva più. Il pover'uomo era in maniche di camicia, e fuori nevicava.
it.source_note: Le avventure di Pinocchio, R. Bemporad & Figlio, Florence, 1902 edition illustrated by Carlo Chiostri, Project Gutenberg EBook #52484 (official PG mirror), chapter VIII

en.text: After a while he returned. In his hands he had the A-B-C book for his son, but the old coat was gone. The poor fellow was in his shirt sleeves and the day was cold.
en.source_note: The Adventures of Pinocchio, translated by Carol Della Chiesa; Project Gutenberg EBook #500 (official PG mirror), chapter 8

notes: Geppetto sells his only coat to buy Pinocchio his first schoolbook, the spelling book («Abbecedario»). The translation has «the day was cold» where the Italian says «e fuori nevicava» (it was snowing outside).

author: Jane Austen

it.text: La persona, uomo o donna che sia, che non si diverte a leggere un buon romanzo, dev'essere intollerabilmente stupida.
it.source_note: L'abbazia di Northanger, cap. XIV, cura e traduzione di Elena Grillo, Newton Compton, 2011 (ISBN 978-88-541-2881-1), as cited on it.wikiquote

en.text: The person, be it gentleman or lady, who has not pleasure in a good novel, must be intolerably stupid.
en.source_note: Chapter 14, spoken by Henry Tilney; same text in Project Gutenberg eBook #121 (opened via mirror https://gutenberg.pglaf.org/1/2/121/121-0.txt)

notes: Spoken by Henry Tilney.

author: Virginia Woolf

it.text: Ciascuno portava chiuso in sé il proprio passato, come pagine di un libro che conoscesse a memoria. Gli amici potevano soltanto leggerne il titolo.
it.source_note: La camera di Jacob, p. 95; the page bibliography lists only the translation by Anna Banti (I libri della Medusa, Mondadori, 1980)

en.text: Each had his past shut in him like the leaves of a book known to him by heart; and his friends could only read the title
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #5670, ch. 5 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: English excerpt stops at 'the title' (the sentence continues with names: ', James Spalding, or Charles Budgeon, ...'); the Italian on it.wikiquote stops at the same point. Translator inferred from the page bibliography (only edition listed).

author: Virginia Woolf

it.text: Troppo spesso le parole sono state usate, maneggiate, rivoltate, lasciate esposte alla polvere della strada. Le parole che cerchiamo pendono accanto all'albero: con l'aurora le troviamo, dolci sotto le fronde.
it.source_note: La camera di Jacob, p. 139; the page bibliography lists only the translation by Anna Banti (I libri della Medusa, Mondadori, 1980)

en.text: But words have been used too often; touched and turned, and left exposed to the dust of the street. The words we seek hang close to the tree. We come at dawn and find them sweet beneath the leaf.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #5670, ch. 8 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: The English opens with 'But' (verbatim); the Italian excerpt on it.wikiquote omits the conjunction. Translator inferred from the page bibliography.

it.text: Per quanti uomini la lettura d'un libro è stata l'inizio d'una nuova era nella loro vita!
it.source_note: Walden ovvero Vita nei boschi, cap. III 'La lettura', introduzione, traduzione e note di Piero Sanavio, BUR, Milano, 1988 (ISBN 88-17-16654-5), p. 171

en.text: How many a man has dated a new era in his life from the reading of a book.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #205, chapter 'Reading' (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

it.text: Non esistono libri morali o immorali. I libri sono scritti bene o scritti male. Questo è tutto.
it.source_note: Prefazione, p. 1; edizione di riferimento della pagina: Garzanti, 2016 (traduzione di Marco Amante, ISBN 9788811810032)

en.text: There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all.
en.source_note: Preface; same text in Project Gutenberg eBook #174

author: Oscar Wilde

it.text: È assurdo immaginare una regola per cosa si dovrebbe e per cosa non si dovrebbe leggere. Più della metà della cultura moderna dipende da ciò che non si dovrebbe leggere.
it.source_note: L'importanza di chiamarsi Ernesto, a cura di Luigi Lunari, BUR, Milano, 2004 (the only edition of the play in the page bibliography)

en.text: It is absurd to have a hard and fast rule about what one should read and what one shouldn't. More than half of modern culture depends on what one shouldn't read.
en.source_note: Act I, Algernon; in Project Gutenberg eBook #844 the line begins 'Oh! it is absurd...'

notes: Spoken by Algernon. Italian edition inferred from the page bibliography.

it.text: Per produrre un possente libro, bisogna scegliere un tema possente. Non si potrà mai scrivere libro grande e duraturo sulla pulce, anche se molti sono coloro che l'hanno tentato.
it.source_note: Moby Dick, cap. CIV, introduzione, traduzione e note a cura di Pina Sergi, Rizzoli, Milano, 2004 (ISBN 88-17-00329-8), p. 555

en.text: To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and enduring volume can ever be written on the flea, though many there be who have tried it.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #2701, ch. 104 'The Fossil Whale' (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

author: J. D. Salinger

it.text: Quelli che mi lasciano proprio senza fiato sono i libri che quando li hai finiti di leggere e tutto quel che segue vorresti che l'autore fosse un tuo amico per la pelle e poterlo chiamare al telefono tutte le volte che ti gira.
it.source_note: Il giovane Holden, cap. III, pp. 22-23, traduzione di Adriana Motti, Einaudi, Super ET, 2008 (ISBN 978-88-06-19309-6)

en.text: What really knocks me out is a book that, when you're all done reading it, you wish the author that wrote it was a terrific friend of yours and you could call him up on the phone whenever you felt like it.
en.source_note: Chapter 3 (Holden Caulfield)

notes: Holden Caulfield speaking. 'e tutto quel che segue' is in Motti's Italian as quoted. it.wikiquote also has a second, unpaged copy reading 'fosse tuo amico'; the paged 2008 copy ('fosse un tuo amico') is used here.

author: Francis Bacon

it.text: Alcuni libri si debbono assaggiare, altri inghiottire, e altri pochi masticare e digerire.
it.source_note: Saggi, L, 'Degli studi', traduzione di Cordelia Guzzo, in Scritti politici, giuridici e storici, vol. I, a cura di Enrico De Mas, UTET, Torino, 1971

en.text: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #575 (Essays), 'Of Studies'; also on en.wikiquote (Francis Bacon)

notes: English excerpt ends at 'digested' (the sentence continues '; that is, some books are to be read only in parts...'). The essay first appeared in 1597; text from the 1625 edition.

author: Samuel Johnson
work: Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson (14 July 1763)

it.text: Ognuno dovrebbe leggere seguendo la propria inclinazione; poichè quel che si legge come un compito non è di gran giovamento.
it.source_note: James Boswell, Vita di Samuel Johnson, traduzione di Ada Prospero, Garzanti, Milano, 1954, vol. I, p. 357

en.text: A man ought to read just as inclination leads him; for what he reads as a task will do him little good.
en.source_note: Life of Samuel Johnson, vol. I (14 July 1763)

notes: Johnson's words as recorded by James Boswell. 'poichè' spelled as in the source.

author: Samuel Johnson
work: Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson (6 April 1775)

it.text: Uno scrittore occupa gran parte del suo tempo nel leggere, per poi scrivere: a volte si legge una mezza biblioteca per fare un unico libro.
it.source_note: James Boswell, Vita di Samuel Johnson, traduzione di Ada Prospero, Garzanti, Milano, 1954, vol. II, p. 205

en.text: The greatest part of a writer's time is spent in reading, in order to write: a man will turn over half a library to make one book.
en.source_note: Life of Samuel Johnson, vol. II (6 April 1775)

notes: Johnson's words as recorded by James Boswell.

author: Harper Lee

it.text: Fino al giorno in cui mi minacciarono di non lasciarmi più leggere, non seppi di amare la lettura: si ama, forse, il proprio respiro?
it.source_note: Il buio oltre la siepe, cap. 2, traduzione di Amalia D'Agostino Schanzer, Feltrinelli (the only translation in the page bibliography)

en.text: Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.
en.source_note: To Kill a Mockingbird, Part 1, ch. 2 (Scout)

notes: Scout speaking.

author: Oliver Goldsmith

it.text: Un libro può essere divertente con molti errori o molto noioso pur senza contenere una sola assurdità.
it.source_note: Il vicario di Wakefield, a cura di Enrico Fenzi, traduzione di Barbara Bartoletti, Fazi, Roma, 1995 (ISBN 88-8112-008-9), p. 5

en.text: A book may be amusing with numerous errors, or it may be very dull without a single absurdity.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #2667, 'Advertisement' (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: Goldsmith was Irish, writing in English.

it.text: Un buon romanzo ci svela la verità sull'eroe, ma un cattivo romanzo ci svela la verità sull'autore.
it.source_note: Eretici, traduzione di Cristina Cavalli, Lindau, Torino, 2010, p. 157

en.text: A good novel tells us the truth about its hero; but a bad novel tells us the truth about its author.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #470, ch. XV 'On Smart Novelists and the Smart Set' (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

author: Aldous Huxley

it.text: Le parole possono essere paragonate ai Raggi X; se si usano a dovere, attraversano ogni cosa. Leggi, e ti trapassano.
it.source_note: Il mondo nuovo, p. 59 (Helmholtz), traduzione di Lorenzo Gigli riveduta da Paola Levante, in Il mondo nuovo – Ritorno al mondo nuovo, Mondadori

en.text: Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly - they'll go through anything. You read and you're pierced.
en.source_note: Chapter 4, Helmholtz Watson

notes: Spoken by Helmholtz Watson.

author: J. R. R. Tolkien

it.text: Ma non disprezzare i racconti tramandati per lunghi anni; potrebbe darsi che le nonne rammentino alcune cose che in passato i saggi era bene conoscessero.
it.source_note: Il Signore degli Anelli, La Compagnia dell'Anello, Celeborn, p. 463, Rusconi edition (page bibliography: 'traduzione di Elèmire Zolla, Rusconi'; the Rusconi translation is usually credited to Vittoria Alliata di Villafranca, with Zolla's introduction)

en.text: Do not despise the lore that has come down from distant years; for oft it may chance that old wives keep in memory word of things that once were needful for the wise to know.
en.source_note: Book II, 'Farewell to Lórien', Celeborn

notes: Spoken by Celeborn. The Italian begins 'Ma' (the original sentence begins 'But do not despise...'; en.wikiquote omits 'But'). Italian translator credit on it.wikiquote is ambiguous (see source_note).

author: John Keats
work: Letter to Percy Bysshe Shelley, 16 August 1820

it.text: La mia immaginazione è un monastero e io sono un monaco.
it.source_note: Lettere, a Percy Bysshe Shelley, 16 agosto 1820; the page bibliography lists Il sogno di Adamo. Lettere scelte 1817-1820, a cura di Anna Foch, Oscar Classici Mondadori, 2001

en.text: My imagination is a monastery, and I am its monk.
en.source_note: Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, ed. Sidney Colvin, Project Gutenberg eBook #35698 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: Italian edition inferred from the page bibliography (only Keats letters edition listed).

author: Tennessee Williams
work: The Field of Blue Children (in One Arm and Other Stories)

it.text: Le parole sono una rete per catturare la bellezza!
it.source_note: Il campo dei bambini azzurri, traduzione di Giuliana Beltrami Gadola, in Tutti i racconti (traduzioni di Giuliana Beltrami Gadola e Nora Finzi), Einaudi, Torino, 1966

en.text: Words are a net to catch beauty!
en.source_note: One Arm, and Other Stories (New Directions, 1954), scanned at the Internet Archive and read through its full-text search; same line in the 1948 edition (archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.184596)

notes: In the story the line is written by the character Myra in her notebook.

author: Helene Hanff

it.text: Mi piacciono moltissimo i libri usati che si aprono alla pagina che l'ignoto proprietario precedente apriva più spesso.
it.source_note: 84, Charing Cross Road, letter of 8 December 1949; the page bibliography lists the Archinto edition, 1999 (ISBN 8877682612), translator not named

en.text: I do love secondhand books that open to the page some previous owner read oftenest.
en.source_note: 84, Charing Cross Road (Grossman, 1970), scanned at the Internet Archive and read through its full-text search; same text in the André Deutsch 1971 scan (archive.org/details/84charingcrossro00hele_0)

notes: Perfect for second-hand copies in a home library. Italian translator not named on it.wikiquote.

author: Augustine Birrell

it.text: Le biblioteche non si fanno; crescono.
it.source_note: Da Obiter Dicta; citato in Elena Spagnol, Enciclopedia delle citazioni, Garzanti, Milano, 2009 (ISBN 9788811504894)

en.text: Libraries are not made; they grow.
en.source_note: Obiter Dicta, Second Series, essay 'Book-Buying', Project Gutenberg eBook #21793 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: English essayist and politician.

author: Charles Lamb
work: Last Essays of Elia: Detached Thoughts on Books and Reading

it.text: Mi diletta perdermi nella mente altrui. Quando non vado a passeggio, leggo; sono incapace di star seduto a pensare. I libri pensano per me.
it.source_note: Detached Thoughts on Books and Reading; citato in Dizionario delle citazioni, a cura di Ettore Barelli e Sergio Pennacchietti, BUR, 2013 (ISBN 9788858654644)

en.text: I love to lose myself in other men's minds. When I am not walking, I am reading; I cannot sit and think. Books think for me.
en.source_note: The Works of Charles and Mary Lamb, vol. 2, Project Gutenberg eBook #10343 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror); first sentence also on en.wikiquote (Charles Lamb)

notes: The essay first appeared in 1822 (London Magazine).

author: Charles Lamb
work: Essays of Elia: The Two Races of Men

it.text: La specie umana, secondo la migliore teoria che posso formarmi su di essa, è composta di due razze distinte, gli uomini che prendono a prestito e gli uomini che prestano.
it.source_note: Saggi di Elia, 'The Two Races of Men'; translation not named on it.wikiquote

en.text: The human species, according to the best theory I can form of it, is composed of two distinct races, the men who borrow, and the men who lend.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #10343 (italics removed); also on en.wikiquote (Charles Lamb)

notes: Italian translation source not named on it.wikiquote. The essay is mostly about borrowing money, but later turns to borrowers of books ('those mutilators of collections'), so it suits a lending feature with a smile.

author: W. H. Auden

it.text: Vi sono libri immeritatamente dimenticati; nessuno immeritatamente ricordato.
it.source_note: La mano del tintore, I, 'Leggere', traduzione di Gabriella Fiori, Adelphi, Milano, 2021 (ISBN 978-88-459-8384-9)

en.text: Some books are undeservedly forgotten; none are undeservedly remembered.
en.source_note: The Dyer's Hand, and Other Essays (1962), 'Reading'

notes: English-born, later American citizen.

author: Stephen King

it.text: Ragazzi, il romanzesco è la verità dentro la bugia, e la verità di questo romanzo è semplice: la magia esiste.
it.source_note: It, dalla dedica, traduzione di Tullio Dobner, Sperling & Kupfer, 1986

en.text: Kids, the fiction is the truth inside the lie, and the truth of this fiction is simple enough: the magic exists.
en.source_note: It (1986), dedication

notes: From the dedication of a horror novel, but the line itself is warm and about fiction.

author: Bertrand Russell

it.text: Due sono i motivi che spingono a leggere un libro: uno, per divertimento; l'altro, per vanità.
it.source_note: La conquista della felicità, cap. III, traduzione di Giuliana Pozzo Galeazzi, Longanesi, Milano, 1969, p. 50

en.text: There are two motives for reading a book: one, that you enjoy it; the other, that you can boast about it.
en.source_note: The Conquest of Happiness (1930), ch. 3

notes: Philosopher and essayist, Nobel Prize in Literature 1950. Witty rather than warm.

it.text: Non leggete mai un libro che non sia vecchio di un anno.
it.source_note: Da Società e solitudine; citato in Elena Spagnol, Enciclopedia delle citazioni, Garzanti, Milano, 2009 (ISBN 9788811504894)

en.text: Never read any book that is not a year old.
en.source_note: Society and Solitude (1870), essay 'Books'

author: L. M. Montgomery

it.text: La gente ride di me perché uso dei paroloni. Ma quando hai delle idee grandiose, come fai a non usare parole grandiose, per esprimerle?
it.source_note: Anna dai capelli rossi, cap. II, p. 22, traduzione di Maria Grazia Odorizzi, Nord-Sud Edizioni, 2021 (ISBN 978-88-9308-252-5)

en.text: And people laugh at me because I use big words. But if you have big ideas you have to use big words to express them, haven’t you?
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #45, ch. II (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: Anne Shirley speaking. Canadian author. The English begins with 'And' (verbatim).

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

it.text: Potete leggere Kant da solo, se volete; ma uno scherzo va diviso con qualcuno.
it.source_note: Virginibus puerisque, a cura di Andrea Minucci, Robin Edizioni, 2004 (ISBN 88-7371-052-2)

en.text: You could read Kant by yourself, if you wanted; but you must share a joke with some one else.
en.source_note: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers, Project Gutenberg eBook #386 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: English 'could ... wanted' vs Italian 'Potete ... volete': the translator's choice.

author: Margaret Atwood

it.text: Una parola dopo una parola dopo una parola è potere.
it.source_note: Citato in AA.VV., Il libro della letteratura, traduzione di Daniele Ballarini, Gribaudo, 2019, p. 14 (ISBN 9788858024416)

en.text: A word after a word after a word is power.
en.source_note: Poem 'Spelling', in True Stories (1982 edition scan), read through the Internet Archive full-text search

notes: Canadian poet and novelist. In some printings of the poem the line breaks after the second 'word' ('A word after a word / after a word is power.').

author: Ursula K. Le Guin

it.text: Farò il mio rapporto come se narrassi una storia, perché mi è stato insegnato, sul mio mondo natale, quand'ero bambino, che la Verità è una questione d'immaginazione.
it.source_note: La mano sinistra delle tenebre, incipit; translation not named on it.wikiquote

en.text: I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.
en.source_note: The Left Hand of Darkness (1969), ch. 1 'A Parade in Ehrenrang', p. 1, opening sentence (the paragraph continues)

notes: Italian translator not named on it.wikiquote (incipit section has no edition).

author: Helen Keller

it.text: Nessuna barriera dei sensi mi priva dei dolci e graziosi discorsi dei miei amici libri. Loro mi parlano senza imbarazzo, né difficoltà.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote thematic page 'Libro', attributed to Helen Keller; translation not named

en.text: No barrier of the senses shuts me out from the sweet, gracious discourse of my book-friends. They talk to me without embarrassment or awkwardness.
en.source_note: The Story of My Life, ch. XXII, Project Gutenberg eBook #2397 (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: Italian found only on the thematic page 'Libro', without a named translation.

author: Thomas Carlyle
work: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History: The Hero as Man of Letters

it.text: La vera università di questi giorni è una collezione di libri.
it.source_note: Heroes and Hero-Worship; translation not named on it.wikiquote

en.text: The true University of these days is a Collection of Books.
en.source_note: Heroes and Hero-Worship, lecture V 'The Hero as Man of Letters' (1840); same text in Project Gutenberg eBook #1091

notes: Scottish essayist. Italian translation source not named.

author: Emily Dickinson
work: There is no Frigate like a Book (J1263 / F1286), lines 1-4

it.text: Non c'è Vascello che eguagli un Libro / Per portarci in Terre lontane / Né Corsieri che eguaglino una Pagina / Di scalpitante Poesia -
it.source_note: Traduzione di Giuseppe Ierolli (Emily Dickinson, Tutte le poesie, J1251-1300, emilydickinson.it, bilingual page); the same translation is quoted on it.wikiquote (Emily Dickinson) with lower-case line openings

en.text: There is no Frigate like a Book / To take us Lands away / Nor any Coursers like a Page / Of prancing Poetry -
en.source_note: Original text (Franklin) as printed on Ierolli's bilingual page; attribution and wording confirmed by Wikisource, Poems: Third Series (1896), 'A Book' (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Emily_Dickinson_Poems_-_third_series_(1896).djvu/43), where the 1896 edition prints it as 'There is no frigate like a book / To take us lands away, / Nor any coursers like a page / Of prancing poetry.'

notes: First stanza only (lines 1-4 of 8). Line breaks shown as ' / '. Dickinson's dashes appear as hyphens ' -' on the source page.

author: Lewis Carroll

it.text: una volta o due aveva lanciato un'occhiata al libro che la sorella stava leggendo, ma non c'erano né figure né dialoghi, "e a cosa serve un libro senza figure e dialoghi?" pensava Alice
it.source_note: Incipit, traduzione di Bianca Tarozzi, Le avventure di Alice nel Paese delle Meraviglie – Attraverso lo specchio, La Biblioteca di Repubblica, 2004

en.text: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversations?”
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #11 (Millennium Fulcrum Edition 3.0), ch. I, first paragraph (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: Excerpt from the middle of the novel's first sentence, in both languages (the full sentence is about 300 characters); both texts start lower-case. The Italian sentence continues after 'pensava Alice' with ':'.

author: Ray Bradbury

it.text: Noi non siamo che copertine di libri, il cui solo significato è proteggerli dalla polvere.
it.source_note: Fahrenheit 451, traduzione di Giorgio Monicelli, Oscar Mondadori, Milano, 1966 (the only edition of the novel in the page bibliography)

en.text: We're nothing more than dust-jackets for books, of no significance otherwise.
en.source_note: Fahrenheit 451 as serialized in 1954 (scan at the Internet Archive, read through its full-text search; word split 'signi- ficance' rejoined); the same sentence is quoted from the novel in Joseph Kampff, Ray Bradbury and the Cold War, 2014 (archive.org/details/raybradburycoldw0000kamp), spelled 'dust jackets'

notes: Spoken by Granger, one of the 'book people' who memorise books. Monicelli's Italian is free ('il cui solo significato è proteggerli dalla polvere').

author: Charles Dickens
work: Our Mutual Friend, book I, ch. 3

it.text: Chi sa leggere non guarda un libro, nemmeno se chiuso in uno scaffale, allo stesso modo di chi non sa leggere.
it.source_note: Il nostro comune amico, lib. I, cap. III; the page bibliography lists the translation by Filippo Donini (in I grandi classici della letteratura straniera, Garzanti-L'Espresso, 2000)

en.text: No one who can read, ever looks at a book, even unopened on a shelf, like one who cannot.
en.source_note: Project Gutenberg eBook #883, Book the First, ch. III (gutenberg.pglaf.org mirror)

notes: Translator inferred from the page bibliography (only full translation listed).

author: Neil Gaiman

it.text: Le storie sono ragnatele collegate filo per filo, e si segue ogni storia verso il centro perché il centro è la sua fine. Ogni persona è un filo della storia.
it.source_note: I ragazzi di Anansi, cap. 12, p. 283, traduzione di Katia Bagnoli, Mondadori, Milano, 2007 (ISBN 9788804567967)

en.text: Stories are webs, interconnected strand to strand, and you follow each story to the center, because the center is the end. Each person is a strand of story.
en.source_note: Anansi Boys (William Morrow, 2005), opening of a chapter, scan read through the Internet Archive full-text search; the chapter opening is printed in small capitals ('STORIES ARE WEBS, INTERCONNECTED STRAND TO STRAND,'), given here in normal case; a 2006 printing has 'interconnected, strand to strand'

notes: English-born author, living.

author: W. Somerset Maugham
work: Pride and Prejudice (essay, in Great Novelists and Their Novels)

it.text: Ciò che rende tale un classico non è il fatto che venga acclamato dai critici, analizzato dai professori, studiato nei corsi universitari, ma che i lettori, una generazione dopo l'altra, vi traggano piacere e giovamento spirituale.
it.source_note: Pride and Prejudice (The Atlantic, 1948), trad. it. di Marco Fiocca, in Jane Austen, Orgoglio e pregiudizio, Oscar Mondadori, Milano, 2014 (ISBN 978-88-04-50615-7), p. 385

en.text: What makes a classic is not that it is praised by critics, expounded by professors and studied in college classes, but that the great mass of readers, generation after generation, have found pleasure and spiritual profit in reading it.
en.source_note: Great Novelists and Their Novels (1948), essay on Pride and Prejudice; scan read through the Internet Archive full-text search (line-break hyphen in 'pro- fessors' rejoined)

author: Logan Pearsall Smith

it.text: La gente dice che la vita è la cosa genuina. Io preferisco leggere.
it.source_note: Afterthoughts, n. 6; translation not named on it.wikiquote

en.text: People say that life is the thing, but I prefer reading.
en.source_note: Afterthoughts (1931), section 'Myself'

notes: American-born British essayist. Italian translation source not named.

author: Luis Sepúlveda
work: Un viejo que leía novelas de amor

original.text: Sabía leer. Fue el descubrimiento más importante de toda su vida. Sabía leer. Era poseedor del antídoto contra el ponzoñoso veneno de la vejez.

it.text: Sapeva leggere. Fu la scoperta più importante di tutta la sua vita. Sapeva leggere. Possedeva l'antidoto contro il terribile veleno della vecchiaia.
it.source_note: Il vecchio che leggeva romanzi d'amore, traduzione di Ilide Carmignani, Guanda, 1996 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: He could read! It was the most important discovery of his whole life. He could read. He possessed the antidote to the deadly poison of old age.
en.source_note: The Old Man Who Read Love Stories, translated by Peter Bush, Harcourt Brace 1993 / Harvest-Mariner paperback 1994; text read through the Internet Archive full-text search of the scanned book (same wording in item oldmanwhoreadlov00sepu, Harcourt Brace 1994)

notes: Italian: the app's text is verbatim Carmignani as quoted on it.wikiquote (the passage continues «Sapeva leggere. Ma non aveva niente da leggere.»). English: the app's text («He knew how to read... the antidote against the terrible venom of old age») is NOT Peter Bush's published wording; it looks like a translation of the Italian. Replaced with Bush's text from the scanned Harcourt edition: «He could read! It was the most important discovery of his whole life. He could read. He possessed the antidote to the deadly poison of old age.» (continues «He could read. But he had nothing to read.»). Original Spanish from a scanned 1998 edition on the Internet Archive (publisher given as Penguin in the record; full-text search); there is no es.wikiquote or en.wikiquote page for Sepúlveda. Full-text search URL: https://archive.org/search?query=%22antidote+to+the+deadly+poison+of+old+age%22&sin=TXT

author: Daniel Pennac

it.text: Il tempo per leggere, come il tempo per amare, dilata il tempo per vivere.
it.source_note: Come un romanzo, traduzione di Yasmina Melaouah, Feltrinelli, 2000 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: Time spent reading, like time spent loving, increases our lifetime.
en.source_note: Better Than Life, translated by David Homel, Coach House Press, Toronto, 1994 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search); same wording in the 1999 Pembroke/Stenhouse reprint

notes: A later translation (Sarah Adams, The Rights of the Reader, Walker 2006) reads «By making time to read, like making time to love, we expand our time for living»; the Homel wording is used here.

author: Anatole France

it.text: Non conosco nessuna lettura più facile, più affascinante, più deliziosa d'un catalogo.
it.source_note: Il delitto dell'accademico Sylvestre Bonnard; it.wikiquote cites Elena Spagnol, Enciclopedia delle citazioni, Garzanti, 2009

en.text: I do not know any reading more easy, more fascinating, more delightful than that of a catalogue.
en.source_note: The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard, translated by Lafcadio Hearn (1890), Modern Library edition, scanned on the Internet Archive, p. 8

notes: Quotation books usually give a shortened form («I know of no reading more easy, more fascinating, more delightful than a catalogue»); the text here is Hearn's own wording from the scanned book. The narrator is cataloguing-minded old scholar Sylvestre Bonnard.

author: Marguerite Yourcenar

it.text: Fondare biblioteche è un po' come costruire ancora granai pubblici: ammassare riserve contro l'inverno dello spirito che da molti indizi, mio malgrado, vedo venire.
it.source_note: Memorie di Adriano, traduzione di Lidia Storoni Mazzolani, Einaudi, 1988 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: The founding of libraries was like constructing more public granaries, amassing reserves against a spiritual winter which by certain signs, in spite of myself, I see ahead.
en.source_note: Memoirs of Hadrian, translated by Grace Frick in collaboration with the author, Farrar, Straus and Young, New York, 1954 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search)

notes: Hadrian speaking. Not on en.wikiquote; the English is read from the scanned 1954 first US edition (also in item in.ernet.dli.2015.125737).

author: Jorge Luis Borges

original.text: Que otros se jacten de las páginas que han escrito; / a mí me enorgullecen las que he leído.

it.text: Che altri si vantino delle pagine che hanno scritto; / io sono orgoglioso di quelle che ho letto.
it.source_note: Poesie (1923–1976), traduzione di Livio Bacchi Wilcock, Rizzoli (as cited on it.wikiquote)

en.text: Let others boast of pages they have written, / I take pride in those I've read.
en.source_note: «A Reader», In Praise of Darkness, translated by Norman Thomas di Giovanni, bilingual edition, E. P. Dutton, New York, 1974 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search)

notes: Opening lines of the poem «Un lector». Verse line break shown as « / » (it.wikiquote marks it with « | »).

author: Gabriel García Márquez

it.text: La vita non è quella che si è vissuta, ma quella che si ricorda e come la si ricorda per raccontarla.
it.source_note: Vivere per raccontarla, traduzione di A. Morino (Angelo Morino), Mondadori (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: Life is not what one lived, but what one remembers and how one remembers it in order to recount it.
en.source_note: Living to Tell the Tale, translated by Edith Grossman, Vintage International, 2004 (as cited on en.wikiquote)

notes: The book's epigraph.

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

original.text: Man sollte alle Tage wenigstens ein kleines Lied hören, ein gutes Gedicht lesen, ein treffliches Gemälde sehen und, wenn es möglich zu machen wäre, einige vernünftige Worte sprechen.

it.text: Bisognerebbe [...] ogni giorno almeno ascoltare una canzoncina, leggere una bella poesia, ammirare un quadro e, se possibile, dire qualche parola sensata.
it.source_note: Gli anni di apprendistato di Wilhelm Meister, libro V, cap. 1; the it.wikiquote bibliography names the translation by Isabella Bellingacci, Mondadori, 2013

en.text: One ought, every day at least, to hear a little song, read a good poem, see a fine picture, and, if it were possible, to speak a few reasonable words.
en.source_note: Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship, Book V, ch. 1; this is Thomas Carlyle's translation (1824) — same words in the scanned 1824 edition, https://archive.org/details/wilhelmmeisters00carlgoog

notes: Spoken by the actor-manager Serlo. The Italian on it.wikiquote keeps an editorial «[...]» after «Bisognerebbe»; copied as is. If the app prefers no ellipsis, this quote should be shortened by someone with the book, not here.

author: Jules Renard

it.text: Quando penso a tutti i libri che mi restano da leggere, ho la certezza d'essere ancora felice.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote cites «Letture», vol. 57, 2002; translator not named

en.text: When I think of all the books still left for me to read, I am certain of further happiness.
en.source_note: The Journal of Jules Renard, edited and translated by Louise Bogan and Elizabeth Roget, George Braziller, New York, 1964 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search)

notes: From Renard's Journal (1887–1910); the entry's date is not shown by the sources I read, so year is null. Do NOT use the en.wikiquote wording («...I am sure that I am still happy»): that page is translated from the Italian Wikiquote, not from a published translation.

author: Rainer Maria Rilke
work: Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge

it.text: Oh, ma come si sta bene tra uomini che leggono! Perché non sono sempre così?
it.source_note: I quaderni di Malte Laurids Brigge, traduzione di Furio Jesi, Garzanti, Milano, 1988, p. 28 (as cited on it.wikiquote)

en.text: Ah, how good it is to be among people who are reading! Why are they not always like that?
en.source_note: The Notebook of Malte Laurids Brigge, translated by John Linton, Hogarth Press, London, 1930 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search; same text in the 1959 Hogarth reissue)

notes: Malte in the reading room of the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris.

author: Plinio il Vecchio (Pliny the Elder)
work: Saying reported by Pliny the Younger, Epistulae III, 5

original.text: Nullum esse librum tam malum, ut non aliqua parte prodesset.

it.text: Non esserci libro tanto cattivo, che non potesse in qualche parte giovare.
it.source_note: Giuseppe Fumagalli, Chi l'ha detto?, Hoepli, Milano, 1921, n. 14 (on it.wikisource); also on it.wikiquote, page «Plinio il Giovane», Lettere III, 5

en.text: He used to say that no book was so bad but some good might be got out of it.
en.source_note: Classical Considerations: Useful Wisdom from Greece and Rome, ed. Marie Carducci Bolchazy, Bolchazy-Carducci, 2006; the wording is William Melmoth's translation as revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet (Bell, 1907: https://archive.org/details/letterscaiuspli01bosagoog) and is also in R. M. Leonard, The Book-Lovers' Anthology, 1911

notes: The saying is Pliny the Elder's, recorded by his nephew Pliny the Younger in a letter (Book III published c. AD 101–103), so year is null. Both texts are reported speech («He used to say...», «Non esserci...»).

author: Carlos Ruiz Zafón

original.text: En una ocasión oí comentar a un cliente habitual en la librería de mi padre que pocas cosas marcan tanto a un lector como el primer libro que realmente se abre camino hasta su corazón.

it.text: Un giorno sentii dire a un cliente della libreria che poche cose impressionano un lettore quanto il primo libro capace di toccargli il cuore.
it.source_note: L'ombra del vento, traduzione di Lia Sezzi, Mondadori, 2004 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography); first sentence of a longer quoted passage

en.text: Once, in my father's bookshop, I heard a regular customer say that few things leave a deeper mark on a reader than the first book that finds its way into his heart.
en.source_note: The Shadow of the Wind, translated by Lucia Graves (2004); read in the scanned 2005 Clipper large-print edition (Internet Archive full-text search). en.wikiquote quotes the same translation from «Few things leave...» onwards

notes: Daniel Sempere narrating. Each text is the first sentence of the same passage, copied verbatim.

author: Montesquieu

it.text: Il grande torto dei giornalisti è di parlare solo dei libri nuovi, come se la verità fosse mai nuova. A me sembra che fino a quando non si siano letti tutti i libri antichi, non ci sia alcuna ragione di preferire i nuovi.
it.source_note: Lettere persiane, CVIII, p. 148, Garzanti (the it.wikiquote bibliography lists the Garzanti edition edited by Lanfranco Binni, 2012); translator not named

en.text: The chief fault of these journalists is, that they talk only of new books; as if truth were always new. It seems to me that until a man has read all the old books, he has no right to prefer the new ones.
en.source_note: Persian Letters, translated by John Davidson, London, 1892, vol. 2, Letter CVIII (scanned book)

notes: Usbek on the literary journals of Paris. The Italian is 221 characters (just over the 220 ideal).

author: René Descartes (Cartesio)

it.text: La lettura di tutti i buoni libri è come una conversazione con i migliori uomini dei secoli passati, che ne sono stati gli autori, e anzi una conversazione premeditata, in cui essi ci fanno conoscere soltanto i loro migliori pensieri.
it.source_note: Discorso sul metodo, parte I; this exact form is on the it.wikiquote page «Libro». The same translation on the page «Cartesio» (https://it.wikiquote.org/wiki/Cartesio) is credited to the edition a cura di Adolfo Levi, Luigi Loffredo, Napoli, 1937, p. 10, and there carries editorial «[...]» at both ends

en.text: I was aware that the reading of all good books is indeed like a conversation with the noblest men of past centuries who were the authors of them, nay a carefully studied conversation, in which they reveal to us none but the best of their thoughts.
en.source_note: Discourse on the Method, Part I, in The Philosophical Works of Descartes, vol. I, translated by Elizabeth S. Haldane and G. R. T. Ross, Cambridge University Press, 1911 (scanned book)

notes: Both texts are a little over 220 characters.

author: Franz Kafka

original.text: Ein Buch muß die Axt sein für das gefrorene Meer in uns.

it.text: Un libro dev'essere un'ascia per il mare ghiacciato che è dentro di noi.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote; no Italian translator named (its reference is Nicholas Murray, Kafka, Hachette digital, an English-language biography)

en.text: A book must be the axe for the frozen sea inside us.
en.source_note: Letter to Oskar Pollak, 27 January 1904 (en.wikiquote). The same words are quoted from Letters to Friends, Family, and Editors (tr. Richard and Clara Winston, Schocken, 1977, p. 16) in Louis Begley, The Tremendous World I Have Inside My Head, 2008: https://archive.org/details/franzkafkatremen0000begl

notes: Medium: the Italian wording has no named published translator (it.wikiquote cites an English book), and it.wikiquote dates the letter November 1903, while en.wikiquote and Begley give 27 January 1904. In context the letter speaks of books that hit us «like a disaster»; the single sentence on its own is fine.

author: Mario Vargas Llosa
work: Elogio de la lectura y la ficción (Nobel lecture)

original.text: La lectura convertía el sueño en vida y la vida en sueño y ponía al alcance del pedacito de hombre que era yo el universo de la literatura.

it.text: La lettura trasformava il sogno in vita e la vita in sogno e poneva alla portata del piccolo uomo che ero l'universo della letteratura.
it.source_note: Elogio della lettura e della finzione, Einaudi (publisher's PDF extract, p. 3); translator not named in the extract

en.text: Reading changed dreams into life and life into dreams and placed the universe of literature within reach of the boy I once was.
en.source_note: «In Praise of Reading and Fiction», Nobel Lecture, 7 December 2010, translation by Edith Grossman, © The Nobel Foundation 2010

notes: From the second paragraph of the Nobel lecture (the first says he learned to read at five and that it was the most important thing that ever happened to him). Vargas Llosa died on 13 April 2025. The Einaudi line break «picco-lo» was joined to «piccolo».

author: Michael Ende

it.text: Una Storia può essere nuova eppure raccontare di tempi immemorabili. Il passato nasce con lei.
it.source_note: La storia infinita, cap. XV (Graogramàn), traduzione di Amina Pandolfi, Longanesi, 1981 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: A story can be new and yet tell about olden times. The past comes into existence with the story.
en.source_note: The Neverending Story, translated by Ralph Manheim, Penguin, Harmondsworth, 1984, ch. XV (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search)

notes: Spoken by Graograman to Bastian. The Italian capitalises «Storia» as in the source.

author: Victor Hugo

it.text: Talvolta zappava la terra del giardino, talvolta leggeva e scriveva; e queste due specie di occupazione le chiamava con una sola frase «coltivare il giardino». «L'anima è un giardino», diceva.
it.source_note: I miserabili, Parte I, libro I, cap. V (as cited on it.wikiquote); the page lists several translations and does not say which one this is

en.text: Sometimes he hoed in his garden, at others he read and wrote. He had only one name for both sorts of labor, he called them gardening. "The mind is a garden," he would say.
en.source_note: Les Misérables, vol. I (Fantine), Little, Brown and Company, Boston, 1887, p. 26; translation credited to Sir Lascelles Wraxall in the Internet Archive record (scanned book)

notes: About Bishop Myriel. Medium because the Italian translator is not identified. The English has inner double quotes (escaped in JSON).

author: Joseph Joubert

it.text: Di coloro cui il mondo non basta: i santi, i conquistatori, i poeti e tutti gli amanti dei libri.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote, section «Pensieri», entry of 26 ottobre 1807; the bibliography lists Pensieri in Moralisti francesi (Rizzoli, 2012) and Pensieri per vivere (Guerini, 2008) without saying which one this is

en.text: Those for whom the world is not enough: saints, conquerors, poets, and all lovers of books.
en.source_note: The Notebooks of Joseph Joubert: A Selection, edited and translated by Paul Auster, North Point Press, San Francisco, 1983 (scanned book); also in Paul Auster, Translations, Marsilio, 1997

notes: Medium because the Italian translator is not identified on it.wikiquote.

author: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg

it.text: Leggere significa prendere in prestito; tirare fuori qualcosa di nuovo di ciò che si è letto significa ripagare il debito.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote, section «Osservazioni e pensieri» (scelta, introduzione e traduzione di Nello Saito, Einaudi, Torino, 1975, per the page bibliography)

en.text: To read means to borrow; to create out of one's readings is paying off one's debts.
en.source_note: The Lichtenberg Reader: Selected Writings, translated and edited by Franz H. Mautner and Henry Hatfield, Beacon Press, Boston, 1959 (scanned book); same text in Lichtenberg: Aphorisms & Letters, Jonathan Cape, 1969

notes: Undated aphorism from the notebooks, so year is null. Fits the lending theme loosely (borrowing and repaying).

author: Jorge Luis Borges
work: Historia universal de la infamia (prologue to the first edition)

it.text: A volte credo che i buoni lettori siano cigni anche più tenebrosi e rari che i buoni autori.
it.source_note: Prefazione alla prima edizione di Storia universale dell'infamia (Buenos Aires, 27 maggio 1935), in Tutte le opere, vol. I, p. 441 (Mondadori, I Meridiani; as cited on it.wikiquote; translator not named)

en.text: Sometimes I suspect that good readers are even blacker and rarer swans than good writers.
en.source_note: A Universal History of Infamy, translated by Norman Thomas di Giovanni, E. P. Dutton, 1972, preface to the first edition (scanned book)

notes: Third Borges quote; drop one if the list needs fewer by the same author.

author: Michel de Montaigne
work: Essais, I, 24 («Divers événements de même conseil»)

it.text: Un lettore perspicace scopre spesso negli scritti altrui perfezioni diverse da quelle che l'autore vi ha poste e intravviste, e presta loro significati e aspetti più ricchi.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote thematic page «Lettore»; no edition or translator given

en.text: An able reader often discovers in other men's writings perfections beyond those that the author put in or perceived, and lends them richer meanings and aspects.
en.source_note: Donald M. Frame's translation (The Complete Essays of Montaigne, Stanford, 1958), as quoted in Elizabeth de Mijolla, Autobiographical Quests, University Press of Virginia, 1994, and in Ermanno Bencivenga, The Discipline of Subjectivity (scanned books)

notes: Medium: the Italian has no source on the it.wikiquote thematic page, and the English is read from books quoting Frame, not from Frame's own edition. Chapter I, 24 confirmed by Randolph Runyon, Order in Disorder (2013), which cites «I: 24, 127a; 93» (Frame p. 93): https://archive.org/details/orderindisorderi0000runy

author: Simone Weil
work: Attente de Dieu (letter to Father Perrin)

it.text: Leggo, per quanto è possibile, soltanto ciò di cui ho fame, nel momento in cui ne ho fame, e allora non leggo: mi nutro.
it.source_note: Attesa di Dio, traduzione di Orsola Nemi, Rusconi, Milano, 1972, p. 32 (as cited on it.wikiquote)

en.text: As far as possible I only read what I am hungry for, at the moment when I have an appetite for it, and then I do not read, I eat.
en.source_note: Waiting on God, translated by Emma Craufurd (Routledge, 1951; scanned 1973 reprint on the Internet Archive, full-text search); the full sentence is also quoted in E. W. F. Tomlin, Simone Weil, 1954: https://archive.org/details/simonewell0000ewft_r8z0

notes: From one of her letters to Father J.-M. Perrin, collected posthumously in Attente de Dieu (1950); the book is religious, the sentence is only about reading. The year 1942 is from my knowledge of the letters, not shown by these sources.

author: Sei Shōnagon
work: Makura no sōshi (The Pillow Book), «Pleasing things»

it.text: Mettere le mani su un mucchio di romanzi non ancora letti. Oppure trovare il secondo volume di un romanzo che ci ha molto emozionati, ma di cui finora avevamo ottenuto solo il primo volume.
it.source_note: Quoted under «Cose che rendono felici» in Carla Vasio, Come la luna dietro le nuvole, Einaudi, Torino, 1996, pp. 19-20 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search); the Italian rendering is the one printed in that book, translator not named in the snippet

en.text: Finding a large number of tales that one has not read before. Or acquiring the second volume of a tale whose first volume one has enjoyed.
en.source_note: Quoted under «Pleasing things» in Alberto Manguel, A Reading Diary, 2004 (scanned book); also in D. J. Enright, Interplay, 1995. Probably Ivan Morris's translation (1967), not confirmed

notes: author_died is approximate: it.wikiquote gives her dates as «965/967 – dopo il 1010» (died after 1010, exact year unknown). The Pillow Book dates from around 1000, so year is null. Both passages continue with «But often it is a disappointment» / «Però spesso si rimane delusi», left out here. Medium because both texts come from books quoting the work and neither translator is confirmed.

author: Marco Tullio Cicerone (Marcus Tullius Cicero)
work: Epistulae ad familiares, IX, 4 (letter to Varro)

original.text: Si hortum in bibliotheca habes, deerit nihil.

it.text: Se presso alla biblioteca ci sarà un giardino, nulla ci mancherà.
it.source_note: Giuseppe Fumagalli, Chi l'ha detto?, Hoepli, Milano, 1921, n. 25 (on it.wikisource; same wording on the it.wikiquote page «Biblioteca»). The it.wikiquote page «Marco Tullio Cicerone» has a variant: «Se presso alla biblioteca avrai un giardino, nulla ti mancherà.»

en.text: If you have a garden in your library, everything will be complete.
en.source_note: The Letters of Cicero, translated by Evelyn S. Shuckburgh, vol. III, George Bell & Sons, London, 1899, p. 83 (letter CCCCLXIV, F ix, 4); scanned book

notes: Years are BC (negative numbers). The popular form «If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need» is a paraphrase; not used.

author: Stéphane Mallarmé
work: Remark to Jules Huret, Enquête sur l'évolution littéraire

original.text: Le monde est fait pour aboutir à un beau livre.

it.text: Il mondo è fatto per finire in un bel libro.
it.source_note: Da Sur l'évolution littéraire; it.wikiquote cites Dizionario delle citazioni, a cura di Ettore Barelli e Sergio Pennacchietti, BUR, Milano, 2013

en.text: The world was made in order to result in a beautiful book.
en.source_note: Translated in Frederic Chase St. Aubyn, Stéphane Mallarmé (1969), p. 23, as cited on en.wikiquote

author: Jean Paul (Johann Paul Friedrich Richter)

it.text: Del resto un libro che non valga la pena di essere letto due volte non è neppure degno d'esserlo una volta sola.
it.source_note: Setteformaggi (Siebenkäs), a cura di Umberto Gandini, Frassinelli, 1998 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: [...] and indeed a book which is not worth reading twice is not worth reading once.
en.source_note: Flower, Fruit and Thorn Pieces (Siebenkäs), translated by Alexander Ewing, Bohn's Standard Library, George Bell and Sons, London, 1895 (scanned book)

notes: In the English the sentence begins after a semicolon («...that they may see what they really lack; and indeed a book...»); the «[...]» is mine to mark the cut, the words are Ewing's. «Del resto» in the Italian matches «and indeed». If the app cannot show a leading ellipsis, drop this quote rather than edit it. The year 1796 (first edition of Siebenkäs, 1796–97) is from my knowledge, not from these sources.

author: Voltaire

it.text: I libri più utili sono quelli i cui lettori compiono essi stessi metà dell'opera; sviluppano i pensieri di cui si mostra loro il germe; correggono ciò che sembra loro difettoso, e fortificano con le loro riflessioni ciò che appare loro debole.
it.source_note: Dizionario filosofico, prefazione; it.wikiquote cites the 2012 edition: Tutti i romanzi e i racconti e Dizionario filosofico, traduzioni di Paola Angioletti e Maurizio Grasso, Newton Compton, 2012

en.text: The most useful books are those of which readers themselves compose half; they extend the thoughts of which the germ is presented to them; they correct what seems defective to them, and they fortify by their reflections what seems to them weak.
en.source_note: Voltaire's Philosophical Dictionary, Carlton House, New York (undated; the Internet Archive record says 1900), Preface (scanned book); translator not named on the scanned pages

notes: Both texts are a little over 220 characters (still under 300).

author: Marguerite Yourcenar

original.text: Le véritable lieu de naissance est celui où l'on a porté pour la première fois un coup d'oeil intelligent sur soi-même: mes premières patries ont été des livres.

it.text: Il vero luogo natio è quello dove per la prima volta si è posato uno sguardo consapevole su se stessi: la mia prima patria sono stati i libri.
it.source_note: Memorie di Adriano, Einaudi, Torino, 1984 (scanned book, Internet Archive full-text search; the Einaudi translation is Lidia Storoni Mazzolani's, as listed on it.wikiquote); also quoted in Il futuro dei libri, vol. 1, Biblioteca del Senato, 2017

en.text: The true birthplace is that wherein for the first time one looks intelligently upon oneself; my first homelands have been books.
en.source_note: Memoirs of Hadrian, translated by Grace Frick in collaboration with the author, Farrar, Straus & Giroux, 1984 edition, p. 33 (as cited on en.wikiquote)

notes: Second Yourcenar quote.

author: Gabriel Zaid

it.text: I veri colti sono capaci di possedere migliaia di libri non letti senza perdere la calma o il desiderio di averne di più.
it.source_note: From So Many Books, as quoted in Nick Hornby, «Il senso della vita», Internazionale, n. 560, 8 ottobre 2004, p. 67 (as cited on it.wikiquote)

en.text: In contrast, the truly cultured are capable of owning thousands of unread books without losing their composure or their desire for more.
en.source_note: So Many Books: Reading and Publishing in an Age of Abundance, translated by Natasha Wimmer, Paul Dry Books, Philadelphia, 2003 (scanned book); also quoted in Nick Hornby, The Polysyllabic Spree, 2004

notes: Mexican essayist, living as far as I know. The English keeps the book's opening «In contrast,»; the Italian (via Hornby's column) starts at «I veri colti». Year left null: the Spanish book first appeared in 1972 and was expanded later, which these sources do not show. Ideal for a home-library app.

author: Quinto Orazio Flacco (Horace)

original.text: Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci, Lectorem delectando, pariterque monendo.

it.text: Ottiene la generale approvazione chi unisce l'utile al dolce, dilettando e istruendo al tempo stesso il lettore.
it.source_note: it.wikiquote cites Giuseppe Fumagalli, Chi l'ha detto?, Hoepli

en.text: He has won every vote who has blended profit and pleasure, at once delighting and instructing the reader.
en.source_note: H. Rushton Fairclough's Loeb translation (Satires, Epistles and Ars Poetica, 1926), as quoted and credited in Elizabeth McCutcheon, My Dear Peter: The Ars Poetica and Hermeneutics for More's Utopia, 1983 (scanned book); same words in The Classical Weekly, 16 May 1932

notes: Years: Horace died 8 BC (negative number); the Ars poetica is usually dated c. 19–10 BC, so year is null.

author: Daniel Pennac

it.text: Una lettura ben fatta salva da tutto, compreso da se stessi.
it.source_note: Come un romanzo, traduzione di Yasmina Melaouah, Feltrinelli, 2000 (edition named in the it.wikiquote bibliography)

en.text: The act of reading, when well done, preserves us from everything, including ourselves.
en.source_note: Better Than Life, translated by David Homel, Coach House Press, Toronto, 1994 (scanned book)

notes: Third Pennac quote; drop one if the list needs more variety. Sarah Adams' later translation reads «A well-chosen book saves you from everything, including yourself.»

author: Marcel Proust

it.text: In realtà, ogni lettore, quando legge, è il lettore di se stesso.
it.source_note: Il tempo ritrovato, traduzione di Giuseppe Grasso, in Alla ricerca del tempo perduto, Newton Compton, 1990, p. 2350 (as cited on it.wikiquote; first sentence of a longer passage)

en.text: In reality every reader is, while he is reading, the reader of his own self.
en.source_note: Remembrance of Things Past, translated by C. K. Scott Moncrieff, Terence Kilmartin and Andreas Mayor, Random House, 1981, as quoted in Inge Crosman Wimmers, Poetics of Reading, Princeton, 1988 (scanned book); also in Alain de Botton, How Proust Can Change Your Life, and S. Gilbar, The Reader's Quotation Book

notes: Both texts are the first sentence of the same passage (it continues: the writer's work is a kind of optical instrument offered to the reader). Le Temps retrouvé was published posthumously in 1927.

author: Jean-Paul Sartre

it.text: Ho cominciato la mia vita come senza dubbio la terminerò: tra i libri
it.source_note: Le parole, trad. it. di Luigi De Nardis, Il Saggiatore, Milano, 2020, p. 33, as quoted in «Diacritica», VII, 39, 31 luglio 2021 (scanned issue, Internet Archive full-text search); the same words, lower-case, in Elena Madrussan, Ricerche di Pedagogia e Didattica 12, 3 (2017), citing the Il Saggiatore edition, p. 31

en.text: I began my life as I shall no doubt end it: amidst books.
en.source_note: The Words, translated by Bernard Frechtman, George Braziller, New York, 1964, as quoted and credited in Nathan A. Scott, The Unquiet Vision: Mirrors of Man in Existentialism, 1969 (scanned book); the same words appear in the scanned 1964 edition (https://archive.org/details/wordssatre0000jean)

notes: The Italian source prints it inside «...» followed by «!» that belongs to the article, so the Italian text has no final full stop; add one only if the app requires it. Frechtman's «amidst books» is also quoted elsewhere as «among books»; the 1964 wording is used.

author: Mario Vargas Llosa
work: Elogio de la lectura y la ficción (Nobel lecture, opening)

original.text: Aprendí a leer a los cinco años, en la clase del hermano Justiniano, en el Colegio de la Salle, en Cochabamba (Bolivia). Es la cosa más importante que me ha pasado en la vida.

it.text: Ho imparato a leggere a cinque anni, nella classe di fratel Justiniano, nel Colegio de la Salle, a Cochabamba, in Bolivia. È la cosa piú importante che mi sia successa nella vita.
it.source_note: Elogio della lettura e della finzione, Einaudi (publisher's PDF extract, p. 3); translator not named in the extract

en.text: I learned to read at the age of five, in Brother Justiniano's class at the De la Salle Academy in Cochabamba, Bolivia. It is the most important thing that has ever happened to me.
en.source_note: «In Praise of Reading and Fiction», Nobel Lecture, 7 December 2010, translation by Edith Grossman, © The Nobel Foundation 2010

notes: Second Vargas Llosa quote (the opening sentence of the lecture); it pairs well with the Sepúlveda quote. «piú» is Einaudi's house spelling of «più», kept as printed; the line break «vi-ta» in the PDF was joined. The English apostrophe is typographic (’) on nobelprize.org.
